nodes.label: Tischfield et al. (2010) identified 8 different heterozygous missense mutations in TUBB3, altering 6 amino acid residues, in 29 unrelated families with CFEOM3. CFEOM3 occurred either alone or as part of neurological syndromes that the authors called the TUBB3 syndromes. Each mutation segregated with the phenotype, was absent in the parents of sporadic patients, and was not found on more than 1,700 control chromosomes.

Tischfield et al. (2010) sequenced TUBB3 in probands with CFEOM plus additional neurological symptoms. They identified a heterozygous 1228G>A transition, causing a glu410-to-lys (E410K) substitution, in 6 pedigrees. In each case the mutation arose de novo as sporadic disease or from presumed germline mosaicism.

Tischfield et al. (2010) reported that all patients with the E410K substitution had severe CFEOM3 and congenital facial weakness. These patients also had more severe corpus callosum dysgenesis with mild to moderate intellectual, social and behavioral impairment. The oldest E410K patient developed lower-extremity weakness and sensory loss in the second to third decade, without congenital contractures.

Tischfield et al. (2010) identified a heterozygous de novo 785G>A transition in TUBB3, causing an arg262-to-his (R262H) substitution, in 2 pedigrees. Patients had severe CFEOM3 and congenital facial weakness. They also had congenital wrist and finger contractures, including ulnar deviation of the hand, and developed lower-extremity weakness and sensory loss in the first decade.

Tischfield et al. (2010) identified a heterozygous 1249G>C transversion in TUBB3, causing an asp417-to-his (D417H) substitution, which co-segregated in a dominant fashion in 1 pedigree. Affected members had severe CFEOM3, congenital facial weakness, congenital wrist and finger contractures, and early-onset lower-extremity weakness and sensory loss.

Tischfield et al. (2010) identified a heterozygous 1138C>T transition in TUBB3, causing an arg380-to-cys (R380C) substitution, in 1 pedigree; it arose de novo or from presumed germline mosaicism. The 2 affected sibs had moderate to severe CFEOM3, agenesis of the corpus callosum and anterior commissure, dysmorphic basal ganglia, hypoplasia of the brainstem and mild vermian hypoplasia, and developmental delay.

Tischfield et al. (2010) identified a heterozygous 1249G>A transition in TUBB3, causing an asp417-to-asn (D417N) substitution, which co-segregated dominantly in 4 pedigrees. Most carriers developed lower-extremity weakness and sensory loss in the second to third decade. Some carriers without CFEOM3 developed polyneuropathy, suggesting that TUBB3 mutations can cause an isolated CMT2-like disorder.

In families with isolated CFEOM3, including the 16q-linked pedigrees BN and DP, Tischfield et al. (2010) identified 3 heterozygous TUBB3 missense changes in 15 unrelated pedigrees: 784C>T (R262C) in 11, 904G>A (A302T) in 3, and 185G>A (R62Q) in 1.

Tischfield et al. (2010) reviewed brain MRI from patients with each TUBB3 mutation except D417H; imaging was normal only in the R62Q patient. Common findings were dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, anterior commissure and internal capsule, generalized loss of white matter, and basal ganglia dysmorphisms. No patient had cortical dysplasia or evidence of cortical migration defects. The severity of intellectual and behavioral impairment generally correlated with the severity of corpus callosum dysgenesis.

Tischfield et al. (2010) reported that many patients had aberrant eye movements and Marcus Gunn jaw-winking synkinesis. Orbital MRI in R262C and D417N pedigrees showed hypoplasia of the oculomotor nerve and of the levator palpebrae superioris, superior rectus and medial rectus muscles, with aberrant innervation of the lateral rectus by the oculomotor nerve. Electromyography showed a chronic, predominantly axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy, diagnosed as CMT2 in some patients.

Tischfield et al. (2010) found that phenotypes limited to CFEOM3 and polyneuropathy often segregated in autosomal dominant families, whereas more severe phenotypes typically arose de novo. Severe CFEOM3 with facial weakness, developmental delay, moderate to severe corpus callosum dysgenesis and probably late-onset polyneuropathy predicted E410K. The additional presence of finger contractures, basal ganglia dysmorphisms and early-onset polyneuropathy suggested R262H or D417H.

Tischfield et al. (2010) generated knock-in mice carrying the R262C substitution in Tubb3. Heterozygous mice appeared healthy, whereas homozygotes died within hours of birth. Homozygotes had normal cortical layering but showed anterior commissure defects, corpus callosum agenesis with Probst bundles in 2 of 5, and misguidance of the oculomotor, trochlear and trigeminal nerves. They also had reduced Tubb3 protein, increased microtubule stability, and reduced Kif21a binding to microtubules.

Tischfield et al. (2010) expressed the mutants in reticulocyte lysate. R62Q, R262C, A302T and R380C markedly reduced heterodimer formation, whereas R262H, E410K and D417H/N formed heterodimers that cycled like wildtype. When the 8 substitutions were modeled in yeast, all altered microtubule dynamics and conferred benomyl resistance. R262C/H, E410K and D417H/N reduced plus-end accumulation of the kinesins Kip3p and Kip2p. The authors suggested that the mutations act through dominant effects on microtubule function, and that facial paralysis and polyneuropathy occur only with the 4 mutations that allow heterodimer formation and disrupt kinesin interactions.

Chew et al. (2013) reported detailed phenotypes of 8 unrelated individuals with the TUBB3 E410K substitution, defining the 'TUBB3 E410K syndrome': congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles, facial weakness, developmental delay and intellectual disabilities, and a progressive sensorimotor polyneuropathy confirmed by electrophysiology. The phenotype was expanded to include Kallmann syndrome (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia), stereotyped midface hypoplasia, and in some cases vocal cord paralysis, tracheomalacia and cyclic vomiting.

Chew et al. (2013) found on neuroimaging of individuals with the TUBB3 E410K syndrome a thin corpus callosum and anterior commissure, and hypoplastic to absent olfactory sulci, olfactory bulbs, and oculomotor and facial nerves, supporting underlying abnormalities in axon guidance and maintenance.
Abnormal morphology of the olfactory bulb

Chew et al. (2013) found the de novo heterozygous c.1228G>A mutation in TUBB3, resulting in a glu410-to-lys (E410K) substitution that directly alters a kinesin motor protein binding site, in 8 unrelated individuals with the TUBB3 E410K syndrome. The authors concluded that E410K defines a new genetic etiology for Moebius syndrome, Kallmann syndrome and cyclic vomiting.

Chew et al. (2013) found that the c.1228G>A mutation was absent in DNA from approximately 600 individuals with Kallmann syndrome or isolated or syndromic ocular and/or facial dysmotility disorders who lacked the combined features of the TUBB3 E410K syndrome, highlighting the specificity of the phenotype-genotype correlation and allowing prediction of the mutation from clinical features alone.

Balasubramanian et al. (2015) described a female proband with TUBB3 E410K syndrome who had congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles (CFEOM), facial weakness, intellectual and social disabilities, and anosmia, but who had normal sexual development at puberty and three spontaneous pregnancies. Her 3 affected sons had nonendocrine features similar to their mother but, in addition, had variable features suggestive of additional endocrine abnormalities.

Balasubramanian et al. (2015) found that the female proband carried a de novo heterozygous c.1228G>A (E410K) mutation in TUBB3, which was transmitted to all 3 of her affected sons, representing the first report of autosomal dominant inheritance of this mutation; all previously reported E410K subjects had been sporadic.

Balasubramanian et al. (2015) reported autosomal dominant transmission of the TUBB3 E410K mutation from an affected mother to her 3 sons, noting that this complicates genetic counseling for families with the syndrome.

Nakamura et al. (2018) reported a 31-year-old Japanese woman who had been diagnosed with atypical Moebius syndrome because of congenital facial weakness and extraocular ophthalmoplegia sparing abduction. At age 23 years she had a femoral neck fracture, and studies showed osteoporosis due to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. She also had borderline intellectual disability, cyclic vomiting, syncope with cough, and decreased sense of smell since childhood. Brain MRI showed abnormal morphology of the corpus callosum and pons, with hypoplastic bilateral oculomotor and facial nerves.

In a 31-year-old Japanese woman with features of the TUBB3 E410K syndrome, previously diagnosed as atypical Moebius syndrome, Nakamura et al. (2018) identified a heterozygous c.1228G>A (p.E410K) mutation in the TUBB3 gene by targeted analysis of TUBB3.

Nakamura et al. (2018) concluded that TUBB3 E410K syndrome may be misdiagnosed as atypical Moebius syndrome because of overlapping clinical features, and that genetic analysis for c.1228G>A in TUBB3 is useful to distinguish it from other disorders with congenital external ophthalmoplegia and facial nerve palsy.

Grant et al. (2019) studied 7 unrelated individuals (4 children and 3 adults) with the TUBB3 E410K syndrome. All had a de novo heterozygous TUBB3 c.1228G>A (E410K) mutation. They had intellectual and social disabilities but no cortical malformations. Compared with 22 controls on structural and diffusion MRI, the patients had decreased corpus callosum volume and decreased network efficiency. All patients showed an aberrant corticospinal tract trajectory and absence of the long segment of the dorsal language network on both sides.

Grant et al. (2019) found that the imaging changes in TUBB3 E410K syndrome differed with age. Only the children had widespread decreases in fractional anisotropy, mainly in mid- and long-range tracts, and they had more tracts with decreased fractional anisotropy than the adults. Only the adults had white matter volume loss, which was associated with decreased cortical surface area. The authors proposed that these findings define a TUBB3 E410K neuroimaging endophenotype. They hypothesized that the age-related changes result from microscopic misguided axons within each hemisphere that are pruned during maturation.

Dentici et al. (2020) reported a 3-year-old boy whose complex phenotype included severe bilateral palpebral ptosis that did not respond to eye surgery, psychomotor delay, absent speech, hypogonadism, celiac disease, and cyclic vomiting. Brain MRI showed thinning of the corpus callosum and no evidence of malformative cortical dysplasia.
In a 3-year-old boy with this syndromic phenotype, Dentici et al. (2020) used clinical exome sequencing to identify a de novo heterozygous recurrent mutation in the TUBB3 gene, c.1228G>A (p.E410K).

Dentici et al. (2020) reviewed reported patients with the TUBB3 E410K mutation and compared them with patients carrying other TUBB3 mutations. They concluded that E410K causes a clinically recognizable syndrome of CFEOM3, intellectual disability, and neurologic and endocrine abnormalities, and that it is not associated with the distinct cortical dysplasia caused by other mutations in the same gene.

Dentici et al. (2020) stated that early molecular characterization of TUBB3 E410K syndrome is critical for targeted genetic counseling and for timely neurologic, ophthalmologic, endocrine, and gastrointestinal follow-up.

Mori et al. (2022) reported an 11-year-old girl who had been followed since infancy as having atypical Mobius syndrome. She was born with bilateral ptosis, paralytic strabismus, and facial weakness. At age 7 years, whole-exome sequencing gave a diagnosis of TUBB3 E410K syndrome.

Mori et al. (2022) used whole-exome sequencing to identify the TUBB3 E410K variant in a girl with congenital bilateral ptosis, paralytic strabismus, and facial weakness. She had previously been diagnosed with atypical Mobius syndrome.

Mori et al. (2022) reported that a girl with TUBB3 E410K syndrome had elevated liver transaminases from age 10 years that persisted for almost 2 years. Liver biopsy was suggestive of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). The authors described this as the first case of TUBB3 E410K syndrome accompanied by NASH.

In the patient's liver, Mori et al. (2022) found that TUBB3 was not expressed in the parenchymal nerve fibers, although tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) was. In contrast, an autopsy case of NASH and a normal control both showed coexpression of TUBB3 and TH. The authors suggested that the TUBB3 mutation may be associated with the pathogenesis and progression of NASH.

Jia et al. (2022) described 2 unrelated Chinese Han probands with CFEOM and the TUBB3 E410K variant: an 11-year-old boy (C21) and a 19-year-old woman (C32), neither with a family history. Both had bilateral ptosis, exotropia, limited horizontal and vertical eye movements, corneal exposure, facial weakness, intellectual impairment and impaired gait. On MRI, both had absent or dysplastic olfactory bulbs and sulci, hypoplasia of the oculomotor nerve and extraocular muscles, absent facial nerves, and malformations of the corpus callosum, anterior commissure and lateral ventricles. The boy had cryptorchidism, and infertility was found in the woman at follow-up.

Jia et al. (2022) reported that 3 patients with the TUBB3 E410K or R262H variant (C21, C32 and C52) met the diagnostic criteria for Kallmann syndrome. The authors suggested that TUBB3 may be involved in the pathogenesis of Kallmann syndrome.

Jia et al. (2022) found that CFEOM patients with the TUBB3 R380C, E410K or R262H variant all had multiple congenital craniocerebral and systemic malformations, whereas patients with R262C or S78T had milder, mostly isolated CFEOM. Absent facial nerves and dysplasia of the olfactory bulbs and sulci were associated with the R262H and E410K variants. The authors noted that patients with the 'TUBB3 E410K syndrome' are easily misdiagnosed as having Mobius syndrome.

Using whole exome sequencing confirmed by Sanger sequencing, Jia et al. (2022) identified the heterozygous TUBB3 c.1228C-T variant (E410K) in 2 of 11 Chinese CFEOM probands carrying TUBB3 variants. Both probands were sporadic cases.
